title: Office to Residential Conversion parameters
$comment: Slider granularity is x-step, never multipleOf - see bathtub's schema. Property order is the panel's reading order: the place and its two clocks, then the view, then the street (segment counts, ground floors, the two-hour comparison), then the deal (the sourced office rent first, since it is the number the whole second gate turns on), then the two gates with the score's weights under the threshold they feed, then the crowd's settings. The office rent is an enum of four named stops with x-enum-notes; only the $54 stop has a source.

district.title: District
district.description: Manhattan Community District 1 is the Financial District, Battery Park City, Tribeca and Governors Island. District 5 is Midtown South, which has a newer, deeper and much larger office stock. Both are included and the map crops to the one selected; 'both' shows the pair and the mile and a half between them, since where a study area ends is a choice.

hour.title: Hour of day
hour.description: The day's clock. Walkers move between the subway stations and the buildings on the measured schedule. Only one clock plays at a time: playing the year holds this one, and playing this one holds the year.

year.title: Year
year.description: The model tests the deal at each of six dates and a building converts at the first one where it clears. There is nothing between the dates, so the control steps rather than slides.

colour_by.title: Color by
colour_by.description: What the color means. "Use" is the one to start with: blue is still office, red has become housing.

added_floors.title: Show added floors
added_floors.description: Where a filing recorded stories being added, the roof is pushed up by that many. That is the amount of the change and not its shape: no setback, no courtyard, no new envelope. It only shows for buildings whose record came from the older filing system, because the newer source carries no heights.

streets.title: Streets by walkers
streets.description: Color and widen each street segment by how many walkers cross it in the selected hour. The counts come from the same routed trips as the dots, so they count trips the model sent down a street, not people observed on it. Clicking a segment puts the camera on it at eye height; the button under the map returns to the district view.

ground_floor_p.title: Active ground floors
ground_floor_p.description: The chance that a converted building's ground floor becomes an active frontage (a shop, or a lobby with glass rather than a service wall). Converted buildings are edged in a warm line where the draw comes up active and a dark line where it doesn't. The probability is ours; no dataset here records what a ground floor is used for at building resolution.

compare_hours.title: Compare two hours
compare_hours.description: Draw the crowd at two hours of the same day at once, in two colors, and color the streets by the difference in walkers between them. While this is on, the crowd is colored by hour rather than by role.

hour_b.title: Second hour
hour_b.description: The second hour for the comparison. Defaults to 20:00, so that the default comparison is the morning peak against the evening.

office_rent.title: Office rent
x-enum-notes: The published asking rent: Manhattan Class B and C combined, NYC Comptroller, Spotlight: NYC's Office Market, 14 May 2024, CoStar data as of 30 April 2024. The only stop with a source. B and C are combined at source, so the sandbox doesn't separate them. At this stop nothing converts before 2050.
What a landlord might collect. Asking rent is a list price, and free months and fit-out allowances aren't published, so this stop applies a flat 25% discount. Ours.
A building in trouble: a 40% discount, standing for a half-empty Class C building signing short leases. Ours.
A repositioned building at the top of the B/C band. The Comptroller's Class A figure is roughly $100. Ours.
office_rent.description: The office rent the deal is tested against, at four named stops. The note above the control says whose number the selected stop is. Only the $54 stop has a source.

office_rent_trend.title: Office rent trend
office_rent_trend.description: How office rent changes each year from its starting figure. This is what moves the model through time: a building converts at the first date the residential deal beats the office income it gives up, so a falling office market opens the gate and a rising one holds it shut. The default is a mild decline, which is an assumption. At zero the map is the same in 2025 and 2050.

residential_rent.title: Residential rent
residential_rent.description: What the converted apartments rent for, per square foot per year. One figure for the whole district, so a basement studio and a corner unit forty floors up earn the same. It is turned into a building value with the residential capitalization rate, and it does not change over time.

conversion_cost_sf.title: Conversion cost
conversion_cost_sf.description: What it costs to turn a square foot of office into a square foot of apartment: new plumbing risers, new windows where the code requires them, and a floor plan that has to reach daylight. No published series was verified for this, so it is an assumption. It scales with how badly the building scores, so an awkward building costs up to twice this figure.

cap_rate_office.title: Cap rate, office
cap_rate_office.description: The rate that turns office income into a building value. Market convention rather than a measurement; no published NYC series was verified. It defaults equal to the residential rate, which makes the two sides of the comparison scale together. In reality office and residential buildings trade at different yields, and the gap is part of why anyone converts, so pulling the two apart is where this control does its work.

cap_rate_residential.title: Cap rate, residential
cap_rate_residential.description: The rate that turns residential income into a building value. Market convention rather than a measurement; no published NYC series was verified. Equal to the office rate by default.

opex_share.title: Operating cost
opex_share.description: The share of gross rent that goes to running the building before any of it counts as income. Ours, and applied the same to an office tower and to the apartments it becomes, which is a simplification. No published NYC series was verified.

min_units_for_conversion_sample.title: Unit floor in the conversion sample
x-enum-notes: 442 filings, 1,366 sf per apartment. No floor: every filing that made a business building residential counts, including one-unit cases that report a whole tower's floor area against a single apartment.
149 filings, 1,152 sf per apartment. The default: conversions of ten units or more.
59 filings, 907 sf per apartment. Only conversions of fifty units or more.
min_units_for_conversion_sample.description: Which real conversion filings the floor-area-per-apartment figure is measured from. A filing records the whole building's floor area rather than the converted part, so including small conversions pulls the average up. Only the six measured cuts are offered, because a value between them would be invented rather than measured. The choice moves the figure by 40%.

convertibility_threshold.title: Convertibility threshold
convertibility_threshold.description: How high a building's convertibility score has to be before conversion is considered. The score is ours: a weighted sum of the four proxies above, with three of the published criteria left out because nothing available measures them. The weights are relative (divided by their total), so what matters is which is heaviest. The legend marks where this threshold would sit for the score to call a quarter of the district convertible, the one figure the consultancy published, and that mark moves with the weights.

w_depth.title: Weight: floorplate depth
w_depth.description: How much the depth from core to window counts in the convertibility score. It is the heaviest weight, which is our judgment. The proxy is MapPLUTO's building depth halved, which assumes a centered core and a rectangular floor plate.

w_f2f.title: Weight: floor-to-floor
w_f2f.description: How much ceiling height counts: the room to run new services under a floor and still have a room. The proxy is the modeled height divided by the number of stories, which averages lobbies and mechanical floors in with the rest.

w_area.title: Weight: floorplate area
w_area.description: How much a small floor plate counts. The proxy is floor area divided by stories.

w_age.title: Weight: age
w_age.description: How much a building's age counts, standing in for the kind of facade it has. Age used to also stand in for the structural bay, which it doesn't measure; that criterion is now listed as missing instead.

incentive_467m.title: 467-m eligibility rules
incentive_467m.description: The state tax exemption for office-to-residential conversion. Its published eligibility tests are applied when this is on: at least 90% non-residential before conversion, six or more units, a quarter of them affordable. Its benefit schedule (the exemption percentage and duration) is not published, so it can't be given a value and is treated as permission rather than money. Off, the tests aren't applied and no benefit is added either. The difference between the two settings is what the rules exclude, not what the money is worth.

agent_count.title: Agents
agent_count.description: How many walkers stand in for the district's day. This is a sample for the eye, not a count: the measured flows are the same at any setting, and even the maximum is about a twelfth of the people the counts say pass through.

schedule_source.title: Schedule
x-enum-notes: Times drawn from the MTA origin-destination curves: October 2024 weekdays, counted at the turnstiles.
Times drawn from four bell curves shaped by the controls below. Their defaults are read off the measured curves, so this starts where the data is.
schedule_source.description: Where each walker's arrival and departure times come from: the measured MTA curves, or four bell curves you can shape with the controls below.

resident_schedule.title: Residents' day
x-enum-notes: Residents leave and return on curves from the American Time Use Survey's weekday diaries of people not employed, which puts them on the street through the day. A national survey, not a New York count.
Residents run the workers' commute in reverse: out in the morning, back in the evening. This is all the subway counts alone can say.
resident_schedule.x-disabled-note: the parametric schedule sets its own
resident_schedule.description: Where residents' times come from. The subway counts aren't split by who is riding, so the mirrored option treats residents as the workers' commute in reverse. The ATUS option gives residents their own day from a national time-use survey, not a New York count.

arrival_median.title: Arrival median
arrival_median.description: The time by which half the morning's arrivals have happened. In the measured curve (October 2024 weekdays) it is 08:47.

arrival_spread.title: Arrival spread
arrival_spread.description: How wide the morning peak is, in hours.

departure_median.title: Departure median
departure_median.description: The time by which half the evening's departures have happened. In the measured curve it is 17:28.

departure_spread.title: Departure spread
departure_spread.description: How wide the evening peak is, in hours.
